title: SLO & Traffic Walkthrough — acceptance checklist and measurement plan
summary: POC scoping to align on TTFT vs TPOT SLOs, traffic sampling plan, measurement methodology (replay + synthetic), bench variants, and acceptance checklist. Agreed to run a 2-stage benchmark (smoke + full sweep) with 10k sample requests across 3 payload buckets, instrumented traces and KV cache on/off. Next: Redwood to share bench scripts and pilot config; Peregrine to provide sample traffic and security contact.
topics: SLO targets (p95 / p99) per payload bucket
Sampling methodology: production replay vs synthetic
meeting_header: Date: 2028-03-16 | Time: 15:00 UTC | Duration: 62 min | Recording: Enabled
transcript: [00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): okay hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, i'll be running point on the pilot — with Arjun who will own the bench and technical run. quick intros?
[00:12] Lena (Peregrine): hi yep lena here, head of ml — we're really focused on response latency for our triage assistant. we want to avoid user-facing lag, obviously.

[00:20] Rajiv (Peregrine Infra): rajiv — infra. ours is k8s on aws right now, but we also have a private GCP project. security-wise we need KMS integration and audit logs, later we'll share contacts for that.

[00:35] Arjun (Redwood SE): great — just to set expectations, we'll propose both TTFT and TPOT SLOs. quick defs: TTFT equals time-to-first-token (time until first byte of model output). TPOT is total per-token time (roughly end-to-end per-token rate averaged across output), sometimes we call it per-token tail too. folks okay with those terms?
[00:58] Sophie (Peregrine PM): yes good. can you run through why we might pick one over the other?

[01:05] Arjun: sure. TTFT matters for perceived latency — chat apps and streaming clients feel faster when first token arrives quickly. TPOT matters for throughput and cost per completion — long responses magnify per-token overhead. For our use case — mixed short/medium replies — we usually set both, with different targets per bucket.

[01:40] Lena: we have three main prompt buckets: short (ack + short guidance ~ <40 tokens), medium (200-400 tokens), long (800+ tokens for discharge summaries). want SLOs for all three. p95 and p99 are what our SLAs require. We care more about p99 on short prompts because that's customer-facing, but medium/long need reasonable p95s.
[02:05] Maya: noted. Arjun, what numbers do you typically see on hosted runs for short prompts?

[02:11] Arjun: depends on model/quantization but ballpark: TTFT p95 ~ 150-300ms for short prompts on optimized runtimes; p99 maybe 350-600ms. TPOT p95 per-token for streaming generation often 30-60ms per token depending on batch and GPU. But key is traffic shape and caching — prefix KV cache can reduce TTFT for repeated patterns dramatically.

[02:45] Rajiv: our current average latency for small microservices is ~120ms. if p99 reaches 600ms users will notice. we want to target TTFT p95 <= 250ms and p99 <= 450ms for shorts — is that realistic?
[03:01] Arjun: it's aggressive but achievable with batching tuned and caching on, plus a model variant we can run on Redwood Dedicated. We'll propose a test matrix to validate.

[03:16] Maya: let's talk concrete acceptance criteria. propose: short prompts (<=40 tokens) TTFT p95 < 250ms, p99 < 450ms; medium (200-400) TTFT p95 < 400ms, p99 < 700ms; long (800+) TTFT p95 < 700ms. For TPOT, per-token p95 target of 45ms for medium/long. Thoughts?
[03:45] Lena: those numbers align with product requirements. can you break out TPOT into p95 per-token and also total completion time p95, because total latency matters for long summaries?
[03:58] Arjun: yes we'll measure both. TPOT per-token p95 as you said, and total completion p95/99 across outputs. We'll also report tokens/s and end-to-end CPU/GPU utilization.
[04:20] Sophie: how many samples do you need to make p99 stats meaningful?

[04:25] Arjun: for p99 with 95% CI we'd like 5k-10k samples per bucket. practical plan: smoke run (1k samples) then full sweep (10k). also do concurrency ramps to emulate bursts — e.g., 1rps baseline, 25rps, 100rps bursts depending on commit size.
[04:50] Rajiv: we can produce a 24h replay of production traffic redacted; does Redwood accept that format?
[04:57] Maya: yes, we can ingest replay traces. prefer gzipped ndjson with request timestamps and prompt hashes. we'll provide a template. also synthetic generators for tail cases.
[05:10] Lena: we have PII in some prompts, will that be an issue?
[05:13] Maya: please scrub or provide synthetic equivalents. for Private deployments we can run in your VPC so data doesn't leave your network. we'll add the security contact in the next steps.

[05:30] Arjun: measurement plan: 1) baseline small smoke with 1k per bucket 2) full sweep 10k per bucket with production replay + synthetic tail injection 3) variants: caching on/off, quantized run, batching policy x2, and routing to Dedicated vs Hosted 4) metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, total completion p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, GPU utilization, queueing latency, and percent of requests hitting cache. We'll also capture traces for cold-start cases.
[06:05] Sophie: can you clarify batching policy x2?

[06:09] Arjun: small clarification — by x2 I mean two batching policies we want to test: low-latency (min-batch-size 1, max-delay 8ms) and throughput (allow batching up to batch-size 32 with 20ms max delay). we'll name them low-latency vs throughput.
[06:35] Lena: what about model variants? we want the best quality but cost matters. can we compare 8-bit quantized vs float16?

[06:42] Arjun: yes — bench both fp16 baseline and int8 / 4-bit quantized where supported. Redwood Optimize will provide quantization profile suggestions, and we'll measure any quality regression on a small eval set Lena provides.
[06:58] Rajiv: instrumentation — we need to correlate app traces with model traces. what headers should we propagate?
[07:04] Arjun: propagate x-request-id and x-trace-span. We'll include a lightweight client library snippet to add them automatically. For Private we'll turn on deeper tracing (jaeger) if you want.

[07:20] Maya: i'm going to read the acceptance checklist aloud so we're aligned: 1) TTFT and total completion SLOs defined per bucket (we just did) 2) Sampling plan: smoke + full sweep with 10k samples per bucket 3) Variants: cache on/off, quant, batching policies x2, Dedicated vs Hosted routing 4) Instrumentation: request id, traces, token-level timing 5) Security: provide scrubbed replay or run in private VPC 6) Timeline: smoke in week 1, full sweep week 2 and 3. anyone needs to change?
[07:55] Lena: timeline works if we can commit to supplying sample traffic and eval prompts by end of the week.
[08:02] Sophie: yes we can have that by Friday. also please include a short doc on sample size math so our compliance folks are comfortable with p99 claims.
[08:14] Arjun: will do. quick note on sampling math: p99 stability needs large n — 10k is a pragmatic tradeoff; we'll provide confidence intervals and show bootstrapped error bars in the report.
[08:30] Rajiv: what are the hardware profiles you'll run on? we might need to see both A100-style and an Ampere cheaper variant.
[08:37] Arjun: planned profiles: 1x A100 for gold-standard, 1x H100 equivalent for high-throughput, and a quantized variant on lower-memory GPUs. We'll provide exact instance SKUs in the runbook.
[08:52] Maya: also note cost buckets: we'll estimate per-token cost across variants so product can assess economics vs quality.
[08:58] Lena: also can we include a stress test to evaluate graceful degradation? i.e., when capacity exhausted do you fall back to a faster model variant or region?

[09:06] Arjun: yes we'll include a fallback test. Redwood supports policy-based routing, so we'll simulate a capacity constraint and measure end-to-end behavior — including any 503s, fallback latencies, and error rates.
[09:25] Sophie: on evaluation, we want to see quality metrics. what do you need from us?

[09:30] Arjun: a small evaluation set per bucket with human labels for correctness/fluency for medium and long replies. we'll run automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE not ideal but a placeholder) plus human inspection on samples where quantization changes outputs.
[09:50] Lena: ok we'll provide 200 eval prompts and 50 hand-labeled long summaries.

[09:55] Maya: good. timeline recap: Friday — Peregrine sends sample traffic + eval set + security contact. Next Monday — Redwood shares bench scripts, runbook, and a short sample-size doc. Wednesday — smoke run; Friday — smoke report. Week after — full sweep begin. Does that sequence look right?
[10:18] Rajiv: yes, except we want the smoke run on Tuesday morning our time, if possible, because Monday is release day. can that be shifted?
[10:25] Maya: yes we can move smoke to Tuesday. We'll update timeline in calendar invite.
[10:32] Sophie: one more question — for replay, how do you handle time-of-day traffic spikes replication?
[10:38] Arjun: we annotate timestamps in replay and allow you to stitch traffic so spikes are preserved. We'll also run synthetic burst tests to amplify tails beyond production to stress the system.
[10:55] Lena: action item: security needs to review private run options. we'll loop in Mark from security.

[11:05] Arjun: noted. Also note measurement nuance: TTFT when streaming can be affected by how the client buffers — we'll provide guidance for client-level streaming buffer sizes and chunk thresholds so your frontend doesn't add latency on top of TTFT. sometimes the model emits quickly but the client waits for a chunk size before rendering.
[11:30] Maya: good catch. we'll include client config suggestions in the runbook. okay do we have any blockers?
[11:38] Lena: only that we need assurance on KMS and audit log retention — i'll send contact. otherwise aligned.
[11:45] Maya: perfect. i'll summarize next steps and action items now.
[11:50] Arjun: quick heads-up — we'll label each benchmark trace with metadata: model_variant, batch_policy, cache_state, concurrency_level, and a run-id so post-processing is easier.
[12:05] Sophie: can you share a sample CSV of the final report? product wants the SLO table in a simple CSV.

[12:11] Maya: yes we'll attach a template. final note: competitors — if you'd like we can add comparative numbers vs Anthropic/OpenAI on similar prompts but that's an optional addon because it increases test scope and cost.
[12:28] Lena: optional is fine but not necessary for this pilot. ok thanks everyone. looking forward to the run.
[12:33] Maya: thanks all — recap in calendar invite and i'll send the bench repo link and runbook by Monday. meeting adjourned.
[12:40] (recording stops)
[61:00] End of meeting
